sourceDesc.p: Song Frontier Translation Glossary , extended for the Warring States chronology.

sense.def: the rulers of the states, collectively; in this period the kings of the warring states and the lesser lords, as distinct from the Zhou king.
to form the 合纵 (hezong) alliance, the north–south ("vertical") league of the eastern states against Qin; 从 stands for 纵.
picked, first-rate soldiers.
commander of an army; used as a title before the name.

form.orth: knock the head to the ground

sense.def: the kowtow of submission or apology, touching the forehead to the ground.
a town or settlement with its lands; the units in which a domain was counted.
"mouths": the registered population, counted by head.
the nine bronze tripod cauldrons held to have been cast by Yu and passed from dynasty to dynasty as the emblem of legitimate rule; their removal to Qin in 256 BC marks the end of Zhou.
to cut off the heads of enemy soldiers; the Qin annals give battle results as a count of heads taken.
the basic unit of direct administration, capitalized as an administrative unit.
enemy killed (counted by head) and taken prisoner, reported together as one figure.
a walled place.
to march to the aid of a state or place under attack.
the designated successor of a king.
a son of a ruling king or lord.
guests kept at a lord's table; the clients of a great house.
men of the gentleman class, from whom officers and retainers were drawn.
a gentleman who withholds himself from office.
gentlemen of worth living in private, without office.
the split tally, often in the form of a tiger, of which ruler and general each held a half; a command was valid only when the halves were matched.
the commander-in-chief.
literally a bath-and-ablution town: a town whose revenue was assigned to a person for private expenses.
a minister of foreign origin at the Qin court.
the chief minister of a state.
households assigned to tend a tomb and keep up its sacrifices.
Sima Qian's own title, introducing his appraisal at the end of a chapter.
the emperor.
a hostage sent to another court as surety.
the five lords who in turn led the states in the Spring and Autumn period.
the founders of the Xia, Shang and Zhou.
the lands east of the Xiao mountains: the states other than Qin.
agents sent to sow division at an enemy court.
the policy of individual states allying with Qin, east to west; the opposite of the Vertical.
the north–south league of the eastern states against Qin.
the nomadic people of the northern steppe.
one holding a Magistrate's post temporarily.
the officer in charge of a County.
the largest territorial unit of a state, above the County.
the governor of a Commandery.
a holder of a fief granted by a king.
the mother of a reigning king.
the principal wife of a king.
a consort of a king below the rank of Queen.
the altar of the god of the soil of a state or settlement.
put to death publicly, the body exposed in the market.
the chief minister, addressed by his full title.
a lord whose land lies inside Qin's passes: a dependant of Qin.
the altars of a state's gods of soil and grain, standing for the state itself.
the temple of a ruling house's ancestors.
the title above king, claimed by Qin and Qi in these years.
literally one in hempen clothes: a man without rank.
the officer in charge of an heir's upbringing.
a state bound by treaty.
the measure of a great state's strength; a ruler of ten thousand chariots is a king.
the whole inhabited world.
a fortified pass.
the chief minister of Chu, the lingyin.
a man in government service below the rank of official; a clerk or functionary.
the sacrifice to Heaven offered by a ruler at an altar outside the city.
the supreme deity, Shangdi, to whom the suburban sacrifice is made.
a rank of royal consort below the Queen; Xu Guang: the title of a secondary wife.
a high office of Chu, next in rank to the Chief Minister (令尹).
the unit in which sums of gold are reckoned: a yi 镒 under the Warring States and Qin, a jin 斤 under Han.
a rank of officials below the ministers (卿).
the head of the administration; the fuller form of the title the texts also write as 相.
the silk ribbon by which the seal of office was hung from the belt.
the office of Chancellor of State held provisionally.
the holder of a marquisate, the fief named before the title.
a retainer attached to a lord's household.
a lodging on the roads for travellers on official business.
the highest grade of a lord's retainers.
to seal a covenant by smearing the lips with the blood of the victim.
the office of Chancellor held provisionally (守); the Biography of Lian Po writes 假相国.
the title conferred on a ruler after his death, by which he is thereafter named.
the title of the ruler of the Xiongnu.
a Hu people north of Dai (Ru Chun).
the Hu people east of the Xiongnu, on Yan's and Zhao's northern frontier.
the Hu people of the forests on Zhao's northern frontier.
the office of a general in the field, under tents (幕); written 莫 for 幕.
the office of Chancellor held provisionally (假); the Biography of Lian Po writes 假相国.
the highest rank of minister (卿).
the household, the unit by which a fief's population and revenue were reckoned.
the title as written in Warring States inscriptions; Han texts write 相国, avoiding the name of Gaozu, Liu Bang.
a straight double-edged blade mounted on a long haft, often inscribed with the year and the officials who oversaw its making.
the lord who holds the leadership of the Lords.
the head of a small or dependent people, below the rank of king.
a military hospital of a garrison town.
the army unit of the period between regiment and division.
a party of volunteers for an assault from which return is not expected.
a medical officer of the army.
the South Manchuria Railway Company (南滿洲鐵道), the Japanese railway concern in Manchuria.
the Red Cross society.
the naval squadron on the Zhili side in 1924, based at Qingdao and Qinhuangdao.
a navy's landing force.
the forces of the Fengtian clique; also written 奉軍.
the second in command of an army.
the officer commanding a brigade.
the forces of the Zhili clique; also written 直軍.
the officer in supreme command.
the office governing the home territory of Qin about the capital.

a state workshop (工室) of Qin, staffed with convicts and men on labour service; the statute does not say where it stood. A Qin Western Workshop (西工) of Shu Commandery is attested on slips excavated at Zikujie, Chengdu.
the lightest grade of Qin convict labour, 'robber-guard', ranking between commoners and the lichenqie 隶臣妾 slaves; by Han law a term of two years.
a person pardoned after a mutilating punishment and set to work out of public sight, 'the hidden'; a status ranked with the sikou.
performing in person one's turn (更) of statutory labour service for the government, as against hiring a substitute.
the five mutilating punishments of the ancient codes: tattooing, cutting off the nose, cutting off the feet, castration and death.
the two swords of legend, forged for the King of Wu by the smith Ganjiang and his wife Moye; the type of a fine blade.
one of the eight steeds of King Mu of Zhou; the type of a fine horse.
the itinerant counsellors who sold rulers plans of war and alliance.
the style a ruler gave a minister honoured as a father, after Duke Huan of Qi's for Guan Zhong (Zhengyi).
the bondsmen of a great house.
a master of argument; a travelling rhetorician.
the palace punishment, 宫刑; 腐罪, an offence punished by it.
one attending within the palace.
a castrated servant of the palace.
a court attendant of the king's entourage; the office, as distinct from 士, the gentlemen as a class.
the chief secretary of a minister or office.
the sage rulers before the Three Kings.
the common people, the Qin term.
the chief judicial officer of Qin.
the title the King of Qin took in 221 BC.
the address to the ruler, literally "beneath the steps".
the women's quarters of the palace, literally the "rear palace".
Han, Zhao, Wei, Chu, Yan and Qi, the eastern states facing Qin.
the lands east of Hangu Pass, the eastern states.
the Yi peoples of Chu's lands (Suoyin); a set phrase for the southern peoples.
the middle period of Shang archaeology, between the Erligang and Yinxu periods.
the first of the four phases of the Yinxu (Anyang) period, corresponding to the reigns of Pan Geng to Wu Ding.
the Bronze Age culture of the Ordos named from the Zhukaigou site, Ejin Horo Banner, and the people who bore it.
the li tripod with applied snake-like strips, the type vessel of the Zhukaigou culture.
the polities around the Shang, so named in the oracle-bone inscriptions.
a fang state of the west against which Wu Ding sent armies.
the Zhou as a fang state in the oracle-bone inscriptions.
the divination records of the Shang kings on turtle plastron and ox bone.
the late Shang-period culture of the Qishui valley named from the Zhengjiapo site, Wugong, Shaanxi.
the local type of Shang culture in the Zhouyuan region, named from the Jingdang site, Fufeng.
the cultural type of the upper Jing valley named from the Sunjia site, Binzhou.
the archaeological culture of the Zhou before the conquest of Shang.
the lands west of the Shang, as the oracle-bone inscriptions call them.
the fang state named Fang 方 in the oracle-bone inscriptions, a people of the north-west under Wu Ding.
